title: Replacing a rotted deck board
subtitle: Remove and replace a single softwood deck board in an existing timber decked area
excerpt: How to remove a rotted or damaged deck board and replace it with a new treated timber board. Covers removing the old board, checking the joists, cutting the new board to length, and securing it with stainless screws.
sourceNotes: Collins Complete DIY Manual (referenced, not reproduced). UK decking trade practice.

glossaryTerms.definition: The horizontal timber that the deck boards are fixed to. On a standard domestic deck, joists are typically 75 x 47 mm pressure-treated C16 structural timber, spaced at 400 mm centres. Joists should be checked for rot before fixing new boards: any softness or discolouration at the joist surface indicates the joist also needs replacing.

content.text: A single rotted deck board can be removed and replaced without disturbing the rest of the deck. The job is straightforward when the screws have not rusted solid. You need to find where the board ends fall on the
and inspect the joists beneath before fitting the replacement.

Drive a chisel under the rotted board and prise it free. If the fixing screws are rusted, drill their heads off with a metal drill bit and lever the board off the screw shanks. If the board ends sit over a joist rather than between joists, saw through the board with the crosscut saw 15 mm from the joist centre on both sides so the new board can be fixed to the same joists.

With the board removed, prod the exposed joist surfaces with a screwdriver or the tip of the chisel. Firm resistance indicates sound timber. Soft, spongy resistance indicates rot. A joist with significant rot must be replaced before new decking is fixed; fitting a new board onto a rotten joist will only delay the same failure.
Cut and treat the replacement board

Measure the gap and cut the new board to length from pressure-treated deck board, matching the original width and thickness. Apply end-grain preservative to all sawn ends as soon as they are cut. For boards stamped UC3 rather than UC4, brush preservative onto all four faces; UC4 is rated for outdoor and high-moisture use.

Set the new board in place with the grooved (anti-slip) face upward and a 5 mm gap at each side to the adjacent boards (a 5 mm spacer or a 5 mm drill bit shank works well as a gap guide). Pre-drill clearance holes through the board at each joist crossing to prevent splitting. Fix with 65 mm stainless steel decking screws driven at a slight angle into the joist top.

attrs.symptom: Replacement board looks conspicuously lighter than the surrounding deck
attrs.cause: New pressure-treated timber is greener or paler than weathered deck boards.
attrs.fix: The colour difference fades naturally after one season. Applying a deck oil to the entire deck (old and new boards) immediately after replacement evens out the tone faster.

attrs.symptom: Board ends split when screwed near the end
attrs.cause: No pilot hole drilled before inserting the screw.
attrs.fix: Always pre-drill a clearance hole at board ends. Use the same diameter as the screw shank (not the thread diameter).
